explanations.explanation: This neuron is picking up on inline emphasis markers—specifically the double‐asterisk (“**…**”) tokens used to bold or highlight text (e.g. Markdown/BBCode style emphasis) across different languages and contexts.
This feature detects boilerplate legal‐ese—copyright and licensing disclaimers, usage restrictions, warranties-as-is, affiliate notices, etc.

explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on sentence‐level discourse pivots—contrastive or emphatic connectors and stance markers (e.g. “but,” “or,” “and,” “personally,” “naturally,” “undoubtedly”) that writers use to signal a turn, highlight a point, or stake out their position.

This neuron is essentially a “hyphen-boundary” detector: it lights up on the internal hyphens (and their immediate context) that join multi-part tokens—e.g. Urbana-Champaign, 2014-06-29, non-muscle-invasive, etc.

This neuron picks out the “hard news” lead signals in a journalistic style text—i.e. the verbs of official action (orchestrate, announce, delegate, commence, file, etc.) and the temporal anchors (days of the week, month names, dates) that typically open a news‐wire report.

This neuron is a “continuation” detector: it fires on BPE subword pieces that occur inside a word (i.e. non‐initial, mid-word fragments across languages) rather than on standalone or space-prefixed tokens.

This neuron seems to flag “heading/metadata” tokens that kick off content sections—things like titles, list numbers or bullets, dates, “Posted by/Published by,” call-to-action verbs (“Download,” “Watch,” “Browse”), etc. In other words, it detects the structural markers used to introduce headers, labels or list items rather than the body text itself.

This neuron fires on the “.” token when it’s acting as a structured delimiter in numeric or abbreviated contexts (decimal points, monetary formats, times like a.m./p.m., date and other abbreviations).

This neuron lights up on the “.” token when it appears mid‐sentence as an internal dot—e.g. in abbreviations (U.S., Mrs., St., John F. Campbell) or as a decimal point in numbers (1.2 million, $2.75 billion) rather than as a sentence-ending full stop.

This feature is a “structural‐boundary” detector—it lights up on tokens that mark the start of a new segment or heading (e.g. the first word after a bullet or paragraph break) and on delimiting punctuation like slashes in “and/or” constructions.
This neuron lights up on the capitalized “lead‐in” tokens that mark the start of headings, titles or list entries—in other words, the initial uppercase word of a structured section or bullet point.

This neuron fires on adverbial “degree‐of‐extent” markers and similar modifiers—words and phrases that qualify or intensify statements (e.g. so/almost/exactly, somewhat, drastically, largely, increasingly, finally, much, little, etc.). It flags those discourse‐level cues that signal how strongly, how much, or in what manner something is being described.

This neuron isn’t tracking a single topic at all but rather “content-word salience” – it lights up on open-class, high-information tokens (nouns, adjectives, verbs, wh-words, brand and technical terms, etc.) that carry the semantic weight of a sentence, and stays quiet on low-content function words.

This neuron is essentially flagging “continuation” subword pieces—i.e. BPE tokens that start in the middle of a word (no leading space), such as common suffixes, abbreviations, numbers or punctuation fragments.
This neuron fires on the very start of long, morphologically complex words—i.e. the subword prefixes or root onsets of multi-syllable terms (in-, un-, de-, inter-, appre-, etc.).
This neuron is a sentence‐boundary detector: it spikes on end-of-sentence punctuation (periods, question-marks, etc.) and/or the very next token at the start of a new sentence.

This neuron fires on the very first token of a short announcement, headline or label—typically an uppercase multi-letter fragment or acronym (e.g. “Cong-” in Congratulations, “Rh” in Rhoneigr, “Invest” in Investigation Discovery, “SK” in SKALD). In other words, it flags the opening, title-style word or prefix at the start of a piece of text.

This neuron fires on closed‐class “head” words that introduce subordinate or embedded phrases—e.g. complementizers (that, though), infinitival to, prepositions (by, as, in, about, including) and auxiliaries (has/have)—marking the start of a clausal or prepositional attachment.
This neuron fires on the very first word of a new entry or section—essentially flagging the start of an article/heading or topic sentence.

This neuron is firing on those short, highly-capitalized or title-case chunks that kick off headings or product/category names (e.g. “Gr” in Grinder, “Br” in Brushes, “Ch” in Chairs/Charts, “Qu” in Quote, “Dec” in Decals, C- and D- prefixes in Cakes or Drip, even CJK ideographs starting Chinese headings). In other words, it detects the initial token of a section title or product name.
